item.title: What can functional transcranial Doppler ultrasonography reveal about the cerebral lateralization of writing.
item.description:
FEBS letters
Written language is central to modern life, yet its cerebral lateralization remains far less understood than that of oral language. This review synthesizes evidence from five functional transcranial Doppler ultrasonography (fTCD) studies (n = 268; 228 adults and 40 children aged 7-9 years), a method well-suited to studying writing due to its tolerance of natural movement. The linguistic component of writing has been shown to be left-lateralized in right-handers, mirroring oral language, whereas for left-handers findings remain inconclusive. Linguistic processing appears largely independent of whether words are produced by hand or keyboard. The unresolved issue is dissociating linguistic from motor components as writing movements may themselves be intrinsically linguistic. Future research should address underexplored populations and leverage writing as a model for neuroplasticity.

item.title: Behavioral dimensions and white matter organization in early childhood following preterm birth
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Background: Children born preterm are at increased risk for attentional, social and emotional challenges, collectively referred to as the preterm behavioral phenotype. While white matter alterations have been linked to individual behavioral domains following preterm birth, it remains unclear whether distinct dimensions of behavioral variability are associated with specific patterns of white matter organization. Understanding neurobiological risk markers for preterm phenotypic traits may help identify children at greatest risk. Objective: We investigated the extent to which these behavioral traits covary across the gestational age spectrum and whether latent behavioral dimensions are associated with white matter micro- and macro-structure in young children born preterm. Methods: We collected behavioral and diffusion MRI data from 58 children born preterm (29 females; mean age = 5.64 ± 0.99 years; GA range = 24-36 weeks) and 85 full-term children aged 4-8 years (44 females; mean age = 5.91 ± 0.95 years; mean GA = 39.26 ± 1.24 weeks). Principal component analyses were performed separately in preterm, full-term, and combined groups to characterize latent behavioral dimensions spanning autism-related traits, ADHD symptoms, and emotional functioning. Fixel-based analysis was then used to examine associations between behavioral dimensions and fiber density and fiber cross-section, adjusting for demographic and perinatal factors. Results: In the preterm sample, autism- and ADHD-related behaviors emerged as relatively distinct dimensions, whereas behavioral variance in the full-term sample was captured by a broad neurodevelopmental dimension. In children born preterm, higher scores on the ADHD-related behavioral dimension were associated with reduced fiber cross-section in the splenium of the corpus callosum. No significant associations were found for fiber density in the preterm or full-term samples. Conclusions: These findings suggest that prematurity influences not only behavioral outcomes, but also how those outcomes relate to white matter organization, highlighting the importance of considering behavioral heterogeneity when investigating brain-behavior relationships in preterm populations.

item.title: ERP markers of language processing difficulties in extremely preterm children at 6-9 years of age.
item.description:
Child neuropsychology : a journal on normal and abnormal development in childhood and adolescence
Advances in neonatal care have substantially reduced mortality among extremely preterm children (≤1,500 g at birth), although survivors remain at increased risk for neurodevelopmental vulnerabilities. This study examined event-related potentials (ERPs) associated with print processing and language-related functions in extremely preterm children at school age. Twenty-six extremely preterm children completed a same/different distractor task involving graphical symbols, illegal letter strings, legal pseudowords, and real words. ERP components indexing print sensitivity (N1), lexico-semantic access (N400), and sensitivity to orthographic regularities (late positive component, LPC) were analyzed across two age groups reflecting early reading initiation and reading acquisition stages. Print sensitivity (N1) exhibited typical developmental patterns in both age groups. However, lexico-semantic access (N400) and orthographic regularity sensitivity (LPC) diverged from patterns reported in studies with typically developing peers, suggesting atypical neural responses to linguistic stimuli despite a presumed adequate behavioral performance. Extremely preterm children may display subtle but meaningful differences in neural mechanisms supporting reading and language processing. These findings highlight the importance of early monitoring and targeted educational interventions to support reading foundations and prevent emerging academic difficulties.

item.title: Brain structural features of treatment resistant depression in a large Italian sample: A multimodal imaging study.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Major depressive disorder is a common psychiatric condition characterized by persistent low mood, emotional dysregulation, and cognitive impairments affecting daily functioning. Approximately 30% of patients fail to respond adequately to at least two antidepressant trials, a condition known as treatment resistant depression (TRD), the neurobiology of which is still poorly understood. This study therefore aimed to investigate grey matter (GM) and white matter (WM) alterations associated with treatment resistance, directly comparing patients with TRD, treatment-sensitive depression (TSD), and healthy controls (HCs). MRI data were acquired from 294 individuals with MDD (193 TRD and 101 TSD) and 72 HCs. Group differences were assessed using analyses of variance followed by post-hoc t-tests. Compared with TSD patients, TRD patients showed reduced GM volume in striatal, temporal, and medial orbitofrontal regions. Relative to HCs, TSD patients exhibited localized GM reductions in the anterior cingulate cortex, whereas TRD patients showed extensive reductions across frontal, temporal, parietal, and limbic areas. Significant differences also emerged in WM microstructural integrity, as measured by fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AD), radial diffusivity (RD), and mean diffusivity (MD). Compared with both TSD patients and HCs, TRD patients exhibited widespread FA reductions paralleled by increased AD, RD, and MD values, whereas no significant differences emerged between TSD patients and HCs. These findings provide evidence that TRD is characterized by a distinct neurobiological profile, offering new insights into the mechanisms of treatment resistance that may ultimately facilitate the development of more effective, tailored therapeutic interventions.

item.title: Principles of coarse-scale functional organization in occipitotemporal cortex.
item.description:
Communications biology
Occipitotemporal cortex (OTC) is known to support visual object processing, yet identifying general principles underlying its coarse-scale functional organization remains challenging. Previously proposed organizational dimensions, such as animacy or real-world size, may not generalize to more diverse, naturalistic stimuli and strong intercorrelations of object properties complicate determining which dimensions, if any, dominate OTC organization. We addressed these challenges through detailed analyses of the cortical topography underlying 15 object properties, using fMRI responses to thousands of natural images, focusing on animacy and size given their established prominence. Our results confirm many characteristics of the purported animacy-size organization, but reveal distinctions that challenge dominant notions of this organization, highlighting the importance of generalizing to large-scale naturalistic data. Beyond animacy and size, many properties could alternatively serve as organizational dimensions, yet none emerges as clearly dominant throughout OTC. Together, our findings reveal a more refined animacy-size organization than previously assumed and highlight challenges of assigning individual principles to account for OTC organization.

item.title: Creative cognition in frontotemporal dementia and brain health.
item.description:
Trends in neurosciences
Creative cognition is central to human thought and is affected by brain disease. Recent findings by Altmayer and colleagues link creative impairment in frontotemporal dementia to rostral prefrontal functional differentiation. These findings motivate a framework for investigating network coordination, circuit physiology, experience-dependent plasticity, and bodily and social regulation in creativity and health.

item.title: When Defense Becomes Compulsion: An Evolutionary and Circuit Framework for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is characterized by intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviors that are frequently organized around preventing potential harm. Although existing neurobiological models have focused on abnormalities in cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits, habit formation, and cognitive control, they provide a less complete explanation for why compulsions preferentially take the form of precautionary actions. Here, we propose an evolutionary and circuit-level framework in which compulsive behavior is understood as a pathological dysregulation of neural systems that normally support adaptive defense. Integrating evidence from human studies with circuit-level findings from rodent studies, we organize defensive control into three sequential but interacting stages: threat appraisal, defensive action selection and execution, and post-defense safety assessment. During threat appraisal, abnormalities in sensory salience, threat valuation, contextual gating, and interoceptive processing may increase the salience or threat value of ambiguous cues. During action selection and execution, intolerance of uncertainty, impaired behavioral flexibility, corticostriatal dysfunction, and negative reinforcement may bias behavior toward premature and repetitive threat-reducing actions that can become increasingly habitual. Following defensive action, impaired outcome evaluation and safety-state updating may prevent successful actions from generating stable signals of safety or completion, allowing defensive responding to persist despite objective threat reduction. By organizing OCD-related circuitry according to when it contributes to defensive processing rather than solely where abnormalities occur, this framework integrates threat-based, corticostriatal, habit, and safety-learning accounts into a process-based model of how adaptive defense may transition into persistent compulsive behavior. This framework may help map stage-specific dysfunction onto symptom heterogeneity and guide more targeted interventions.

item.title: The Separation-Distress Network as a Transdiagnostic Mechanism Linking Relational Adversity, Social Pain, and Psychopathology.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Relational trauma is a major contributor to the development of mental health disorders. This association likely reflects the social nature of humans and other mammals, whose survival depends on maintaining stable social bonds. When these bonds are threatened or disrupted, individuals experience social pain, a distress response mediated by the mammalian separation-distress network. During early development, this network is sensitive to maintaining proximity with caregivers, as independent survival is not yet possible. Converging evidence from ethology, psychodynamic and attachment theory, and social and affective neuroscience supports the function of this network. Because mammalian brains are inherently tuned to form social bonds, adverse relational experiences can disrupt socioemotional development and increase vulnerability to psychopathology. Neural substrates of separation distress include the anterior cingulate cortex, ventral septum, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, dorsal preoptic area, dorsomedial thalamus, and periaqueductal gray, with endogenous opioids and glucocorticoids serving as key neurochemical modulators in the separation-distress response. Separation distress and adverse relational experiences also alter physiological systems implicated in psychopathology, including the HPA axis, autonomic nervous system activity, inflammation, and brain structure and connectivity. This paper argues that relational trauma and social pain are mediated by an evolutionarily conserved subcortical separation-distress network shared across predominantly mammalian species. Dysregulation of this network may represent one common mechanism underlying depression, social anxiety, suicidality, substance use disorders, borderline personality disorder, and other psychiatric conditions. Understanding the processes linking adverse relational experiences, separation-distress activation, and social pain may provide insights into the etiology and treatment of diverse disorders.

item.title: Cognitive impairment in age-related hearing loss: linking brain structure, glymphatic function, and molecular mechanisms.
item.description:
Brain research bulletin
The neurobiological mechanisms of cognitive impairment in age-related hearing loss (ARHL) remain unclear. This study examined multi-level neural mechanisms from macroscale gray matter (GM) structure, microscale glymphatic function, and imaging transcriptomics. Sixty-nine ARHL patients and 76 controls underwent multimodal MRI and neuropsychological assessments. Glymphatic function was assessed via DTI-ALPS index and choroid plexus volume (CPV). Transcriptomic analysis using Allen Human Brain Atlas identified molecular pathways and key genes linked to GM atrophy. ARHL patients showed GM atrophy in right amygdala, left inferior frontal gyrus, and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), but increased volume in left cerebellum. They also exhibited reduced ALPS index and enlarged CPV. Mediation analysis showed a significant indirect effect of glymphatic function on visual memory via right amygdala volume. Transcriptomics revealed enrichment in axonogenesis, energy metabolism, and protein ubiquitination, with key drivers including SMURF1 and GAD1. ARHL-related cognitive decline may follow a cascade from sensory deprivation to glymphatic dysfunction, involving energy metabolism, protein homeostasis, and axonal remodeling, ultimately leading to degenerative atrophy and compensatory adaptation in specific brain networks.

item.title: Examining the Relationship Between Regional Vulnerability and Psychotic-Like Experiences in Adolescents: The Potential Mediating Role of Cognition.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
Psychotic-like experiences (PLEs) are subclinical hallucinations or unusual thought content that, when distressing or persistent, signal heightened risk for psychosis spectrum disorders and cognitive impairments. We used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study (N = ∼11,800) to examine if structural brain deviations toward neuropsychiatric disorders, quantified using disorder-specific Regional Vulnerability Indices (RVIs), were associated with distressing PLEs at age 13-14, and whether cognition mediated these relationships. Cortical and subcortical RVIs were calculated for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, metabolic disorder, and 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that higher cortical RVIs for schizophrenia, Alzheimer's disease, bipolar disorder, metabolic disorder, and Parkinson's disease-and all subcortical RVIs-were significantly associated with greater distressing PLE severity. Both cortical and subcortical RVIs were negatively associated with fluid and crystallized cognition, with subcortical RVIs showing the largest effects. Mediation analyses indicated that crystallized cognition, and to a lesser extent fluid cognition, mediated many RVI-distressing PLE relationships. These findings suggest that neuroanatomical differences confer risk for psychotic-like experiences partly through their impact on cognitive development. The results highlight RVIs as sensitive markers of distributed brain vulnerability in youth and suggest that cognitive function, particularly crystallized ability, is a potential pathway linking brain structural alterations to emerging psychotic symptoms.

item.title: Information, Mass, Energy Principles: A biophysical and ecological framework for understanding the brain.
item.description:
Bio Systems
The brain is a highly complex biological system whose structure, function, and evolution are constrained by material resources and energy availability, as any other natural system. Here, we extend the ecological Information-Mass-Energy (IME) framework (Peñuelas, 2024) to neuroscience. In contrast to purely computational models, we propose that the brain is an information-organizing system constrained by mass availability, energetic expenditure, and thermodynamic efficiency. Through comparative analyses across mammalian species, we identify a superlinear scaling relationship between white and grey matter volumes, alongside a positive association between white matter volume and inhibitory-control performance. This suggests that neural organization contribute to cognitive capacities beyond brain size alone. Integrating these findings with metabolic scaling principles, we propose that brain evolution involves trade-offs between increasing informational complexity and the material and energetic costs required to sustain it. Within this framework, we formulate testable hypotheses concerning how informational organization may scale with neural material and energetic expenditure. Furthermore, we introduce a quantitative disturbance-recovery model that incorporates carrying capacity, recovery rate, and disturbance magnitude and duration, generating testable predictions for neurological conditions such as stroke and neurodegeneration. By combining empirical scaling relationships with a mathematical framework for neural organization, energetic constraints, and resilience, the IME framework offers a novel biophysical and ecological perspective on brain evolution and function. This framework also provides a foundation for investigating energetically sustainable information processing in biological and artificial systems.

item.title: Altered EEG-derived co-fluctuation structure in disorders of consciousness.
item.description:
Cognitive neurodynamics
EEG-derived functional connectivity (FC) enables high-temporal-resolution probing of neural mechanisms underlying disorders of consciousness (DOC). Unlike stationary conventional FC, dynamic FC (dFC) captures fast transient neural coupling. Recent fMRI studies introduced a co‑fluctuation framework to track moment‑to‑moment connectivity change, yet whether such co-fluctuation features can quantify consciousness status remains elusive. Here, we adapt this established co-fluctuation paradigm to resting-state EEG to characterize the temporal architectures of EEG-derived FC across varying conscious states. We decomposed the co-fluctuation time series into high-amplitude frames (HAF) and low-amplitude frames (LAF), comparing their dynamics between real brain data and null models. We then analyzed co-fluctuation activities across consciousness levels at both global and local spatial scales, examining spatial variability in these patterns. By integrating HAF and LAF parameters, we evaluated their diagnostic potential for distinguishing DOC states. Results revealed reduced stability of co-fluctuations with loss of consciousness, accompanied by a shift toward random system dynamics. DOC patients exhibited reduced spatial and temporal heterogeneity in co-fluctuation activities compared to healthy controls. Both high- and low-amplitude patterns provided useful metrics for detecting consciousness levels. These findings offer novel insights into the dynamic organization of brain networks in DOC, emphasizing the significance of co-fluctuation dynamics in characterizing brain states and suggesting potential biomarkers for assessing consciousness levels. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11571-026-10580-7.

item.title: Expectation-driven gain modulation of preparatory spatial attention.
item.description:
eLife
The visual system can flexibly adjust attentional deployment to match task demands, but whether observers can proactively modulate the spatial scope of attention based on expectations about upcoming search difficulty remains unclear. According to the zoom lens model, attention can narrow or broaden its spatial extent, with narrower focus enhancing processing efficiency, a mechanism that would benefit target discrimination in crowded displays. We tested whether observers adjust attentional scope when expecting sparse versus dense search arrays by combining spatial cueing with block-wise manipulations of display density expectations. Participants performed a visual search task in which endogenous cues predicted target location, while blocks predominantly contained either sparse (1 target, 3 distractors) or dense (1 target, 7 distractors) displays. We applied inverted encoding models to broadband EEG data to reconstruct spatial channel tuning functions, enabling precise characterization of both the locus and breadth of attentional deployment. Behaviorally, expecting difficult searches selectively improved accuracy at cued locations without costs elsewhere. Consistent with this selective benefit, neural measurements revealed that expectancy enhanced the amplitude of spatially selective responses at the attended location but did not alter tuning width. These findings demonstrate that expectations about search difficulty modulate attention through gain-based signal enhancement rather than adjustments to spatial scope, revealing that preparatory attentional control operates via amplitude modulation within a stable spatial focus. This mechanism complements reactive attentional adjustments and provides an efficient means for the visual system to optimize processing under predictable task demands.

item.title: Greater Stress Response Network (SRN) Connectivity is Associated with Higher Worry in Men and Women Especially in Later Life
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Late-life anxiety is common and disabling, with pathological worry as a core feature. The Stress Response Network (SRN: amygdala, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, paraventricular nucleus), which modulates threat and stress reactivity, and its interaction with the Executive Control Network (ECN), anchored by the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which supports emotional regulation via top-down cognitive control, may underlie individual differences in worry severity. We hypothesize higher SRN connectivity to be associated with greater worry severity and that this relationship may be moderated positively by older age, and female sex. Methods: We recruited older adults with varying worry. Resting-state fMRI was used to compute SRN connectivity and SRN-ECN connectivity. Regression models tested associations between connectivity and worry (PSWQ), anxiety (HARS), and rumination (RSQ), adjusting for age, sex, race, and education. Exploratory models examined age and sex moderation and associations with emotion regulation/suppression and cognitive function. Results: Among 131 participants who were ≥ 50 years old, with varying levels of worry severity, SRN connectivity was significantly associated with greater worry severity (B=23.51 (SE = 12.12), p<0.05), whereas SRN-ECN connectivity was not. SRN connectivity was lower with greater age (B=-0.003 (SE=0.001), p=0.04), yet older individuals reported greater worry than younger with comparable connectivity. Greater language domain cognitive function was associated with lower SRN connectivity but higher SRN-ECN connectivity, while greater overall cognitive function was associated with lower SRN-ECN connectivity. Women reported lower use of daily expressive suppression and higher performance across cognitive measures than men. Higher daily use of expressive suppression was not significantly associated with either connectivity measure. Discussion: SRN connectivity, rather than SRN-ECN connectivity, may serve as the primary neural correlate of worry, shaped by age and cognitive function.

item.title: Learning rapidly reshapes brain microstructure: evidence from dense temporal sampling of diffusion MRI.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Learning is associated with rapid microstructural changes in the human brain, yet the precise temporal dynamics of these changes remain unclear. Using dense temporal sampling of diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI) combined with task-based fMRI, we assessed microstructural changes throughout a declarative learning paradigm and subsequent rest. Seventy-four participants (36 females) learned image-location associations across four encoding-retrieval repetitions while undergoing interleaved functional and DW-MRI acquisitions. A matched control group (N=37, 21 females) underwent a similar imaging protocol without learning. Dense sampling of DW-MRI acquisitions (2146 images across 22 time points in 127 min) revealed that learning-induced mean diffusivity (MD) decreases emerged shortly after learning onset and continued to develop during post-learning rest. The most robust change was localized to the left middle occipital/temporal gyrus, a region also showing functional activation during encoding and retrieval. Linear mixed-effects modeling further confirmed a significant group-by-time interaction, with MD reductions in the left middle occipital/temporal gyrus emerging as early as ≈7 min after learning onset, becoming robust by ≈35-40 min, and persisting throughout the extended post-learning period, while controls showed no changes. Our findings demonstrate that learning-related microstructural plasticity unfolds continuously from encoding to offline consolidation, with learning-induced structural changes emerging in functionally engaged regions. Dense temporal sampling of DW-MRI offers a powerful approach to bridge functional activation and structural remodeling, providing evidence of when and where experience-dependent plasticity occurs during memory formation.Significance Statement How quickly does the brain's structure change when we learn? Using dense temporal sampling of diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI; 2146 images) across more than 2 hours, we show that microstructural plasticity arises rapidly during learning and continues to develop during post-learning rest. These learning-induced changes are spatially precise and overlap with task-related functional activity. By capturing the entire progression of microstructural plasticity across the learning process, rather than just before and after a learning paradigm, our study provides insights into when and where learning-induced plasticity occurs, demonstrating that memory formation involves rapid, ongoing microstructural changes in functionally engaged regions.

item.title: Location matters: The link between regional white matter hyperintensity burden and subjective cognitive decline in those at risk of Alzheimer's disease.
item.description:
Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD
BackgroundSubjective cognitive decline (SCD) is a potential early indicator of Alzheimer's disease (AD). While SCD has been linked to white matter hyperintensity (WMH) burden, it is unclear whether regional WMH lesion volume is differentially associated with domains of cognitive complaints.ObjectiveExamine whether regional WMH burden is associated with domain-specific SCD (memory, executive function) in cognitively unimpaired older adults with a family history of AD.MethodsParticipants were 150 cognitively unimpaired older adults (65-89 years) with subjective memory complaints and a first-degree family history of AD. Cognitive complaints were assessed with the Cognitive Change Index (CCI-20). WMHs were quantified from T1-weighted and FLAIR MRI using an automated pipeline and categorized into sample-based tertiles for total, subcortical, and lobar regions. Hierarchical regressions examined associations between WMH burden and CCI-20 memory, executive, and total scores, while adjusting for demographics, total intracranial volume, MRI site, APOE ε4 status, and mood symptoms.ResultsGreater WMH burden in the left temporal lobe was associated with increased memory complaints and total SCD, whereas no WMH region was associated with executive function complaints. APOE ε4 status and depressive symptoms were associated with greater memory and total cognitive complaints across models. Apathy was uniquely related to memory complaints.ConclusionsAmong older adults with elevated risk of AD, memory-SCD was associated with greater region-specific left temporal cerebrovascular lesion volume. Findings highlight the clinical relevance of left temporal WMH burden and the importance of considering regional vascular pathology, genetic risk, and mood when characterizing early subjective cognitive changes.

item.title: Repeated Exposure to Military Low-Level Blast Is Associated With Regionally Specific Reductions in Gray Matter Volume in Breachers and Snipers.
item.description:
The Journal of head trauma rehabilitation
Objective To examine the association between duration of repeated exposure to low-level blast and alteration in brain structure. Setting Data were collected at 2 neuroimaging facilities. Participants Canadian Armed Forces breachers (n = 30) and snipers (n = 31) with a history of repeated exposure to low-level blast (average years = 9.70, SD = 4.57) and sex- and age-matched active military controls (n = 57). Design MRI and neurocognitive data from breachers and snipers were collected prospectively at baseline (time 1) and after a training exercise involving a concentrated regimen of blast exposure (time 2) (time gap = 80.56 days, SD = 36.90). Time 1 and time 2 data were used to assess the chronic and training-related effects of blast exposure, respectively. MRI and neurocognitive data from controls were collected twice with a comparable time gap. Main measures High-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, plus neurocognitive measures. Results Voxel-based morphometry conducted on MRI data collected at time 1 demonstrated that compared with controls, there was lower regional gray matter volume in left inferior frontal gyrus in snipers, and bilaterally in parahippocampal gyrus (bordering on amygdala) in breachers. Regional gray matter volume in left inferior frontal gyrus in snipers predicted neurocognitive function. We did not observe any difference in regional white matter volume between groups at time 1, nor any changes in regional gray or white matter volume between time 1 and time 2. Conclusion Chronic but not training-related low-level blast exposure was associated with dissociable patterns of regional gray matter volume reduction in snipers and breachers, and regional gray matter volume predicted neurocognitive function in snipers. The differential pattern of structural alteration between breachers and snipers and its relationship with neurocognitive function in snipers can inform health monitoring programs for diagnosis and treatment of blast-exposed service members and Veterans.

item.title: Network disruption in post-stroke depressive symptoms: a Bayesian multicohort study.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Post-stroke depressive symptoms are common, but studies on the contributions of lesion locations to depression symptoms remain inconsistent. Bayesian statistics offer the possibility to clarify these inconsistencies by providing evidence in favor and against observed associations. We reanalyzed four previously published observational cohorts with 1,864 patients with stroke characterized for depressive symptoms from France, Korea, Germany and the USA. We performed voxel-wise Bayes factor mapping using general linear models. Lesion maps were used to test for associations of post-stroke depressive symptoms with lesion location. Network level associations were tested based on structural disconnection and functional lesion network maps estimated by reference to normative connectome data. Due to a sample size with broad lesion coverage, Bayesian inference was informative in large parts of the brain. Lesion associations were found in clusters in the right hemisphere including cortical (frontal, insular, parietal) and subcortical regions (striatum, amygdala, hippocampus) and adjacent white matter. Evidence of no contribution to post-stroke depressive symptoms was observed in large parts of the left hemisphere. Structural disconnection was linked to depressive symptoms in the bilateral frontal white matter prominently involving the corpus callosum and anterior thalamic radiation. Lesion network mapping revealed evidence of an association of post-stroke depressive symptoms with network connectivity in the left posterior cingulate cortex and precuneus, and less consistently, the bilateral anterior insula, along with widespread absence of associations in other regions. Depressive symptoms were most strongly associated with right frontal lesions and right-dominant structural disconnection in frontal cortico-subcortical circuits.

item.title: Respiratory phase orchestrates human olfactory cortical dynamics.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Olfaction is fundamental to perception, memory, and emotion, yet the neural basis of human odor processing remains poorly understood. We demonstrate that odor-evoked brain activity is organized by respiratory phase-not absolute time-revealing that natural breathing structures olfactory cortical dynamics. Using simultaneous nasal respiration and electroencephalography recordings in [Formula: see text] participants, we delivered naturalistic odors (peppermint, oregano, and grapefruit) synchronized to individual breathing cycles. Odor presentation elicited respiratory phase-locked event-related spectral perturbations (RPL-ERSPs) in frontal and temporal regions, emerging during the first breath after stimulus onset. The most discriminative neural signatures were theta-band activity during inhalation and alpha-band activity during exhalation, patterns that were obscured in traditional time-locked analyses due to natural variability in breath duration. Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation of RPL-ERSPs achieved reliable odor detection (peppermint: AUC [Formula: see text] 0.79; oregano: AUC [Formula: see text] 0.67; grapefruit: AUC [Formula: see text] 0.62), establishing that phase-locked features generalize across individuals. To connect neural responses to perceptual experience without relying on odor naming-which can be disproportionately impaired in some populations-we quantified odor recognition using free-response descriptions scored with a semantic-similarity approach. Behavioral recognition strength paralleled the neural decoding hierarchy across odors, establishing the perceptual validity of RPL-ERSPs. RPL-ERSPs revealed rapid habituation, with decoding performance declining over repeated presentations, due to selective degradation of the most informative phase-locked features. These findings establish respiratory rhythm as a temporal scaffold for human olfactory cortical processing, positioning RPL-ERSPs as a sensitive, task-free approach for assessing olfactory function. We provide an open-source, respiration-synchronized olfactometer design to enable replication and adoption.

item.title: Language Experience Modulates Parallel Acoustic and Phonological Processing of Mandarin Tone: Evidence From Mismatch Negativity.
item.description:
Journal of speech, language, and hearing research : JSLHR
PURPOSE: Second-language (L2) speech perception is strongly influenced by prior language experience, but the neural mechanisms supporting this process remain incompletely understood. This study examined how language experience modulates the pre-attentive encoding of acoustic and phonological information in Mandarin tone perception and whether these cues are processed serially or in parallel. METHOD: Twenty native Mandarin speakers and 20 novice Mandarin learners with a tonal first language (L1: Thai) completed a behavioral tone identification task and a passive listening multifeature oddball event-related potential paradigm. Stimuli were drawn from an 11-step Tone 1-Tone 2 continuum with Stimulus 5 (S5) as the standard and Stimuli 1, 3, 7, and 9 as deviants. Deviants varied in fundamental frequency distance (large vs. small acoustic distance from S5) and category status (across- vs. within-category) relative to each participant's own phonetic boundary for the continuum. Temporal principal component analysis was applied to separate early and late mismatch negativity (MMN) components. RESULTS: Behavioral identification did not differ across groups. However, MMN results revealed that both acoustic and phonological factors modulated early and late responses, supporting parallel processing. Native Mandarin speakers exhibited stronger and more sustained phonological effects across both time windows bilaterally. Nonnative speakers showed greater acoustic sensitivity, particularly over the right-hemisphere electrodes, and weaker phonological effects, with reduction most evident over the left-hemisphere electrodes. CONCLUSIONS: The findings show that Mandarin tone perception involves parallel extraction of acoustic and phonological information at the pre-attentive level, with language experience influencing their relative weighting. The neural-behavioral dissociation suggests that tonal L1 experience supports perceptual decisions without fully automatized phonological representations transferred to L2. SUPPLEMENTAL MATERIAL: https://doi.org/10.23641/asha.34925781.

item.title: Constructing events across perception, action, and thought.
item.description:
Trends in neurosciences
The brain organizes continuous experience into events that structure episodic memory and guide behavior. Traditional accounts have primarily focused on sensory discontinuities and prediction errors that trigger updates of event models. Here, we broaden this view to consider event boundaries arising during goal-directed behavior, spontaneous thought, and memory recall, including transitions generated in the absence of corresponding changes in sensory input. We propose that prediction error and uncertainty provide complementary signals for event model updating: prediction errors signal a violation of current expectations, whereas uncertainty may promote updating when upcoming states become difficult to predict. We further suggest that the hippocampus may serve as a candidate hub linking boundary-related representational changes across perception, action, and thought. Together, this framework offers an integrative account of how the brain detects and generates event structure in continuous experience to support memory and behavior.

item.title: Consumer neuroscience: the emerging science of everyday choices.
item.description:
Trends in cognitive sciences
Consumer neuroscience is a developing field at the intersection of neuroscience, psychology, economics, and marketing that seeks to uncover the neural and physiological mechanisms underlying consumer behavior. Building on early psychophysiological studies, the field has expanded substantially since the mid-2000s through an increasing range of methods and models. We highlight that its strength lies in spanning multiple levels of analysis to address marketing-relevant questions. We highlight four major trends driving the field: improving behavioral prediction, synthesizing evidence through multidataset analyses, developing formal models linking neural processes to consumer decision-making, and integrating brain and body measures. Together, these advances position consumer neuroscience as an integrative science with implications for marketing, policy, and consumer welfare.

item.title: Interhemispheric structural connectivity alterations and hierarchical connectome gradient reorganization following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
item.description:
Neuroscience
Neurological sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection extend beyond the acute phase, yet the structural basis of network-level brain changes across disease severity remains poorly understood. We investigated structural brain connectivity and connectome gradient organization in adults with polymerase chain reaction-confirmed coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), stratified into non-hospitalized and hospitalized groups, alongside a comparison group with non-COVID respiratory infection, using 3T diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging. Network-Based Statistics was used to identify subnetworks of altered structural connectivity, and connectome gradients were derived separately for each hemisphere using diffusion map embedding and compared across groups within seven canonical resting-state networks. Network-Based Statistics identified a predominantly interhemispheric subnetwork differing across the three groups, linking left-hemispheric control and salience regions to right hemisphere sensory and association areas, with a related subnetwork distinguishing hospitalized participants from the comparison group. Connectome gradient analysis revealed group-related differences in connectivity-derived embedding positions within sensorimotor and dorsal attention networks, more pronounced among hospitalized participants. These findings suggest that SARS-CoV-2 infection is associated with severity-related interhemispheric structural connectivity differences and altered hierarchical connectome organization, particularly within sensorimotor and dorsal attentional systems. Given the cross-sectional design, modest sample size, and absence of behavioral data, these findings should be considered exploratory and do not establish anatomical fiber loss, causal mechanisms, or predictive clinical value; instead, they provide a structural framework to guide future studies of neurological outcomes after COVID-19.

item.title: Beyond Scene Construction: Mind Time and the Temporal Organisation of Cognition across Hippocampal-Cortical Systems.
item.description:
Neuropsychologia
Scene-construction theory explains how spatially coherent event models support memory and imagination, although parts of their temporal organisation are less fully specified. Mind Time brings scene construction into relation with temporal-context and self-location research, drawing on autobiographical memory and navigation to explain how events are related to one another and to a selected temporal origin across scales. Separating these represented relations from the operations that produce and revise them accommodates evidence for a distributed hippocampal-cortical system, including temporal judgements possible despite impaired episodic construction. Comparative findings constrain inferences about component capacities without resolving claims about subjective experience. Within this integrative account, we propose that, during active construction, revising a temporal relation changes the information available to a represented self within the relevant history before a particular consequence is requested. An experiment would test whether this inferred state changes in advance and is available for use in subsequent imagination. Communication could carry the revision between people; transpersonal extended Mental Time Travel (teMTT) specifies how communication or shared records alter another person's later reconstruction or planning. Existing mental-model and predictive accounts could implement the coordination.

item.title: Working memory supports cognitive control by orchestrating dimension-specific modulation during late conflict resolution.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Working memory plays a central role in cognitive control, yet how it shapes target- and distractor-related processing over time remains unclear. Here, we combined a working memory load manipulation with a modified Stroop task in which distractors preceded targets. Behaviorally, we found that pre-exposure to the distractor eliminated the congruency effect, but this benefit was absent under high load. This pattern suggests that the benefit of advance distractor presentation is sensitive to concurrent working-memory demands. Electrophysiologically, the distractor-locked lateralized readiness potential (LRP) indicated that working-memory load altered distractor-related response activation before target onset. After target onset, load-related modulation emerged during late conflict resolution, as indexed by the sustained potential (SP), whereas earlier intervals associated with attentional selection (posterior N2) and conflict monitoring (N450) did not show load-dependent modulation. Time-frequency decoding and representational similarity analysis further revealed distinct spectro-temporal profiles of target- and distractor-related processing: target-related coding emerged earlier in the theta band (540-780 ms), consistent with stimulus-response mapping, whereas distractor-related coding emerged later in the mu-beta band (870-1180 ms), consistent with response-related regulation. These findings highlight dimension- and stage-specific patterns of working-memory modulation during conflict resolution.

item.title: Short-Video Experience and Brain-State Dynamics During the Processing of Rapidly Changing Video Information in Youth.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Background Short-video platforms frequently expose youth to rapidly changing video information. Processing such inputs requires large-scale brain networks to reorganize with the ongoing context. However, little is known about these dynamics or their association with prior short-video viewing experience. Methods A total of 108 youth aged 8-18 years completed resting-state and naturalistic movie-viewing fMRI scans. The movie comprised rapidly changing and relatively continuous segments. Hidden Markov models were applied to 17 cortical networks to identify recurrent brain states, and a joint rest-task analysis examined the context specificity of the main finding. Results Eight task-related brain states were identified. Five differed in fractional occupancy (FO) between conditions, and global switching was slightly higher during rapidly changing segments. State 7 was the only state showing an interaction with short-video viewing experience. Its FO was higher during relatively continuous than rapidly changing segments among participants reporting no prior Douyin use, whereas the condition difference was not significant among those reporting prior Douyin use. Visit frequency analyses showed a similar pattern. The interaction remained robust after covariate adjustment and was also observed in the joint rest-task analysis, with no significant group difference at rest. Conclusions Rapidly changing video information was associated with brain-state reorganization in youth. Douyin use was associated with lower State 7 occupancy during relatively continuous narrative segments; no significant group difference in the matched state's occupancy was detected at rest. These findings provide new evidence linking short-video viewing experience to context-dependent brain dynamics in youth.

item.title: Associations among interleukin-6, superior frontal gyrus thickness, and executive control in long-term high-altitude migrants.
item.description:
Acta psychologica
This study examined how systemic inflammation, prefrontal cortical structure, and executive control performance are related in long-term high-altitude residents. A total of 129 healthy Han Chinese adults who had relocated from low-altitude regions and were living and working in Lhasa, Xizang (3650 m) underwent hematological testing, structural MRI, and an Attention Network Test (ANT). Serum interleukin-6 (IL-6) concentration was obtained from clinical blood reports, cortical thickness of the left superior frontal gyrus (SFG) was extracted using FreeSurfer, and executive control efficiency was indexed by the conflict effect in the ANT (lower scores indicating better performance). Partial correlations and mediation analyses (PROCESS Model 4) were conducted, controlling for age, gender, and hypoxic exposure duration. IL-6 concentration was significantly negatively correlated with executive control scores (r = -0.22, p = 0.04), indicating that higher IL-6 levels were associated with better executive control efficiency, whereas no significant associations were found with alerting or orienting. Mediation analysis showed a significant indirect effect of IL-6 on executive control via left SFG thickness (indirect effect = -0.024, 95% CI [-0.093, -0.003]), with a significant total effect (-0.218, 95% CI [-0.429, -0.007]) and a nonsignificant direct effect (-0.194, 95% CI [-0.403, 0.014]). These findings suggest that relatively higher IL-6 concentrations within the physiological reference range are associated with better executive control performance, with left SFG cortical thickness showing a significant statistical indirect association. Together, these results highlight a potential immune-structure-cognition relationship in long-term high-altitude migrants, although comparative and longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether these associations are specifically related to high-altitude exposure.

item.title: Resting state functional connectivity associated with maternal anxiety: preliminary evidence that infant rsFC moderates the association between behavioral inhibition and anxiety/depression.
item.description:
European child & adolescent psychiatry
Postnatal maternal anxiety shapes caregiver and infant behavior. Yet, the relationship with infant brain function remains unclear. We examine the relation of maternal anxiety with infant resting state functional connectivity (rsFC). To evaluate the clinical significance of the rsFC networks identified, exploratory analyses tested whether the rsFC associated with maternal anxiety moderates risk trajectories from infant behavioral inhibition (BI) to childhood anxiety/depression symptoms. Four-month-old infants (N = 60) underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and mothers completed the Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI). Analyses included 49 infants with high-quality imaging and maternal anxiety data. In the longitudinal subsample (n = 21), BI was observed at 14 months, and anxiety/depression symptoms were assessed at 4-6 years using the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL). Using whole-brain network enrichment analyses, we identified cortical network pairs that were significantly associated with maternal anxiety. Connectivity estimates from significant network pairs were averaged and tested as moderators of infant BI and childhood anxiety/depression association. Infants exposed to higher maternal anxiety showed an altered limbic-dorsal attention network (DAN) and default mode (DMN)-DAN. In both network pairs, negative and positive node-to-node pairs were identified, indicating that some regional connections exhibited stronger coupling, while others exhibited weaker coupling. Results demonstrated that DMN-DAN rsFC moderated developmental pathways: greater BI was associated with higher early-childhood anxiety/depression among infants with stronger DMN-DAN connectivity. Maternal anxiety is related to infant brain connectivity, and these neural differences moderate BI-related risk for anxiety/depression. DMN-DAN coupling may serve as an early marker of infants at risk for anxiety/depression. Given the small longitudinal sample, the moderation finding should be considered exploratory and requires replication in a larger, independent cohort.

item.title: Distinct neural representations of perceptual and numerical absence in the human brain.
item.description:
eLife
The ability to represent absences is fundamental to human perception and cognition. Sensitivity to non-numerical absences depends on inferring a lack of sensory evidence, enabling the recognition of a lack of environmental resources or other objects. In turn, encoding numerical absence as a concept - in the form of the number zero - has enabled a multitude of technological and mathematical advances. Whether perceptual and conceptual absences rely on overlapping or distinct neural representations in the human brain, however, remains unknown. We employed three different tasks together with magnetoencephalography to characterise neural representations of absence evoked within perceptual and numerical domains. Using multivariate decoding and Bayes factor analyses, we replicate previous findings of shared representations of numerical absence across symbolic and non-symbolic formats. In contrast, we show that these representations of numerical absence are distinct from those evoked by non-numerical absences. This result held even after controlling for stimulus-level confounds which generate surface-level similarities between perceptual absences and non-symbolic empty sets. Our results extend a boundary between perception and cognition to the domain of absence and provide insight into the different mechanisms employed by the human brain to both perceive and conceive of absences.

item.title: Cortical Thinning in Adults with Prader–Willi Syndrome: Distribution Across Functional Networks and Associations with BMI and the GH/IGF-1 Axis
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Prader–Willi syndrome (PWS) is a rare neurogenetic disorder associated with neuropsychiatric, metabolic, endocrine, and physical abnormalities. Although previous neuroimaging studies have identified regional gray matter alterations, cortical thickness (CT) abnormalities and their distribution across large-scale functional brain networks remain poorly characterized in adults with PWS. We investigated cortical morphology in 23 adults with PWS and 22 age- and sex-matched healthy controls who underwent structural MRI. Cortical reconstruction and surface-based morphometric analyses were performed using FreeSurfer. Between-group differences in CT were assessed using age, sex, and intracranial volume as covariates. Associations between CT and clinical, cognitive, anthropometric, and endocrine measures were examined using Spearman correlations. Significant cortical regions were further mapped onto an a priori functional network atlas. Adults with PWS showed reduced CT in a left-hemispheric cluster involving the inferior precentral gyrus, insula, inferior temporal cortex, and orbitofrontal cortex. This cluster overlapped predominantly with the somatomotor, auditory, cingulo-opercular, language, and frontoparietal networks. Within the PWS group, lower CT was associated with higher body mass index and poorer global functioning. CT was positively associated with IGF-1 levels and was greater in participants with a history of growth hormone therapy during childhood. These findings indicate cortical thinning across regions belonging to multiple functional networks involved in sensorimotor, attentional, language, and executive processes, extending previous volumetric findings. The associations with body mass index, functional measures, and the GH/IGF-1 axis suggest that cortical morphology may reflect an interplay between genetic vulnerability and potentially modifiable metabolic and endocrine factors, raising the possibility of a neuroprotective role for GH/IGF-1 signaling.

item.title: Early WM Alterations after Mild Traumatic Brain Injury: An Exploratory Study Using Quantitative MRI and DTI.
item.description:
AJNR. American journal of neuroradiology
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: The purpose was to investigate early WM alterations in patients with mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) within 1 week of trauma using quantitative MRI and DTI. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 31 patients with mTBI and 36 healthy controls. Neuropsychological assessment and MRI scans were performed within 1 week of trauma. ROIs were selected from 4 WM regions: superior longitudinal fasciculus, anterior limb of the internal capsule, posterior limb of the internal capsule, and external capsule. Quantitative MRI and DTI were used to assess WM alterations. Correlation analyses explored relationships between WM alterations and clinical outcomes. RESULTS: Compared with controls, patients with mTBI demonstrated lower scores on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, particularly in the domains of abstraction, delayed recall memory, and orientation. Higher T1 values were detected in the left posterior limb of the internal capsule, whereas elevated proton density (PD) values were found in the right external capsule, bilateral superior longitudinal fasciculus, and posterior limb of the internal capsule. No significant differences in T2 or fractional anisotropy were observed. PD values in the left posterior limb of the internal capsule were negatively correlated with attention and language scores in patients with mTBI. CONCLUSIONS: In conclusion, quantitative MRI may detect subtle WM alterations in the acute stage of mTBI. No notable between-group differences were observed in the DTI parameters in the current cohort. Larger longitudinal studies are needed to determine the reproducibility, temporal evolution, and clinical relevance of these findings.

item.title: Endogenous suspension of phenomenal consciousness during extended cessation: Regional homogeneity analysis of multi-participant 7T fMRI of an advanced meditative endpoint.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Extended cessation (EC) is a rare advanced meditative state characterized by the voluntary absence of reportable phenomenal experience, followed by reproducible aftereffects including immense mental clarity, equanimity, and peace. EC offers an endogenous model for investigating the mechanisms of consciousness. In a small-N case study (N = 3) using ultra-high-resolution 7T functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with dense within-subject sampling, we quantified whole-brain activity and related it to chemoarchitecture and cognitive maps. EC is marked by increased activity in unimodal sensory cortices and viscerosensory brainstem nuclei, and down-regulation in transmodal regions, subcortex and brainstem. Meta-analytic cognitive decoding linked EC to perceptual clarity and attentional processes, and away from distress-related domains. Multivariate coupling to normative neurotransmitter maps revealed that EC-related connectivity changes covaried with histaminergic H3 receptors topology. These findings constrain prevailing theories of consciousness by demonstrating that loss of experience need not entail global neural suppression, and supports accounts emphasizing selective precision modulation and hierarchical decoupling. More broadly, EC demonstrates that consciousness can cease without global suppression, suggesting a potential "reset" mechanism that fosters equanimity and the potential for flourishing.

item.title: In-group neural alignment serves as a biomarker of social identity.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
In this study, we propose a perspective on neural synchronization. Beyond reflecting shared understanding between individuals, we suggest it serves as a biological marker of social homogeneity. We examined fMRI neural responses of 42 participants (21 religious, 21 secular) watching neutral and religion-relevant video narratives. While explicit measures of emotional response, agreement, and engagement showed no significant differences in within-group variance, religious participants-representing a tighter social structure-exhibited significantly higher in-group neural synchrony across all content types and brain networks. Remarkably, synchrony values predicted religious orientation with an accuracy of up to 92%. We conclude that a community's homogeneous social structure drives pervasive neural alignment, positioning neural synchrony as a potential signature of group cohesion beyond explicit behavioral measures.

item.title: Disrupting the semantic network shifts activity to domain-general brain regions.
item.description:
Nature communications
Semantic processing relies on flexible interactions between specialized lexico-semantic regions and domain-general control networks, particularly under challenging conditions. Using transcranial magnetic stimulation interleaved with functional magnetic resonance imaging, we investigated acute network adaptation when the left posterior middle temporal gyrus-a core lexico-semantic region-was perturbed during lexico-semantic decisions in 25 healthy participants. High-intensity transcranial magnetic stimulation over the posterior middle temporal gyrus induced task-specific activity increases across semantic control and lexical retrieval areas, as well as remote domain-general regions. Critically, increased local activity at the stimulation site correlated with slower reaction times, whereas greater upregulation in domain-general frontal regions was associated with less disrupted semantic performance. These findings indicate that acute semantic disruption triggers immediate, flexible recruitment of domain-general control areas consistent with the maintenance of task performance, highlighting the brain's capacity to dynamically adapt to interference. Our findings contribute to the current understanding of putative compensatory network-level mechanisms supporting lexico-semantic cognition.

item.title: Network-based virtual perturbation for modeling DBS-related network effects in obsessive-compulsive and major depressive disorders.
item.description:
Psychological medicine
BACKGROUND: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) efficacy for psychiatric disorders remains heterogeneous due to incomplete mechanistic insights and insufficient individualized treatment planning. A biologically grounded computational framework is urgently needed to simulate DBS-related differences for treatment-resistant patients. METHODS: Resting-state fMRI data from 11 patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and 11 with major depressive disorder (MDD), scanned in DBS-ON and DBS-OFF states, were used to derive functional connectivity (FC) via network deconvolution. Whole-brain dynamic modeling incorporated stimulation targets, amplitudes, and frequencies to simulate DBS effects in silico. RESULTS: The model recapitulated syndrome-specific DBS-related network patterns in exploratory analyses. OCD stimulation primarily altered frontal-subcortical connectivity, whereas MDD stimulation predominantly affected default mode network hubs (p < 0.05). Under leave-one-out cross-validation, correlations between predicted and observed clinical outcomes were r = 0.625 in OCD (p = 0.040) and r = 0.659 in MDD (p = 0.028). Applying the same FC signatures to simulated FC yielded r = 0.465 in OCD (p = 0.149) and r = 0.627 in MDD (p = 0.039). In a proof-of-concept application to a separate OCD cohort (N = 92), three individuals showed high model-predicted NAc-response profiles and predicted improvement exceeding 35%. CONCLUSIONS: This hypothesis-generating framework retrospectively models DBS-related network effects using individualized resting-state FC and virtual perturbations. Linking simulated FC states with empirical DBS-ON/OFF patterns may help characterize how baseline functional architecture shapes DBS-related network responses and inform future individualized DBS modeling.

item.title: Linguistic features from constrained spontaneous speech as potential markers of preclinical Alzheimer's disease.
item.description:
The journal of prevention of Alzheimer's disease
BACKGROUND: Language impairment is an early sign of Alzheimer's disease (AD) that may emerge before more obvious cognitive decline. Linguistic features derived from verbal responses to cognitive tests have shown promise for identifying mild cognitive impairment and predicting AD risk; however, their relationships with established AD biomarkers remain insufficiently characterized. OBJECTIVES: To examine relationships between a comprehensive set of linguistic features derived from logical memory delayed recall (LMDR) responses and amyloid status as well as regional tau burden among cognitively normal participants. DESIGN: In this cross-sectional study, we evaluated associations between two types of AD biomarkers (amyloid status and regional tau burden) and linguistic features using covariate-adjusted regression models tailored to each feature's distribution (e.g., linear, negative binomial, zero-inflated beta, and gamma regression). We then used LASSO regression and the Boruta feature-selection algorithm to identify features most informative of biomarker status. SETTING: A community-based subcohort from the Framingham Heart Study. PARTICIPANTS: A total of 238 cognitively unimpaired participants who completed the LMDR test within 1 year before or after tau positron emission tomography (PET) were included. Of these, 228 also underwent amyloid PET and 227 had LMDR voice recordings available. MEASUREMENTS: Verbal responses to the LMDR test were digitally recorded and manually transcribed. We extracted 54 linguistic and paralinguistic features from transcribed responses using natural language processing, capturing lexical diversity and density, syntactic complexity, semantic/information density, and speech fluency and rate. Tau SUVR values were quantified from PET imaging in 5 brain regions (amygdala, entorhinal cortex, inferior temporal [IT], inferior parietal [IP], and precuneus). Amyloid status was classified as Aβ- or Aβ+ using Gaussian mixture modeling of PiB PET DVR values. LMDR total score and participant demographics (age, sex, education) were included as covariates. RESULTS: After adjusting for age, sex, education, amyloid status, and LMDR score, 23 linguistic features were associated with tau burden in at least one brain region. For example, reduced semantic richness, captured by lower uniqueIdeaDensity, was associated with higher tau burden across multiple regions, including the amygdala (average marginal effect (AME)=-0.007, 95% CI: (-0.013, -0.001)), entorhinal (AME=-0.007, 95% CI: (-0.013, -0.002)), IT (AME=-0.008, 95% CI: (-0.014, -0.002)), and precuneus (AME=-0.006, 95% CI: (-0.012, -1.51e^-5)). More between-utterance pauses were associated with higher tau burden in the entorhinal (AME=0.259, 95% CI: (0.026, 0.493)), IT (AME=0.272, 95% CI: (0.025, 0.518)), and IP (AME=0.404, 95% CI: (0.160, 0.648)) regions. No linguistic features were associated with amyloid status, and LMDR total score was not associated with either tau burden or amyloid status. LASSO regression selected 3-7 features per brain region, capturing multiple aspects of language use (e.g., speech disfluency and semantic density) associated with tau burden. The nonlinear Boruta algorithm selected a larger set of biomarker-informative features, including predictors of amyloid positivity, and identified additional syntactic measures (e.g., Yngve score, mean dependency distance) as important predictors of regional tau burden. CONCLUSIONS: Linguistic features derived from neuropsychological (NP) tests capture subtle language changes associated with regional tau pathology in cognitively normal individuals, beyond conventional NP test scores. These findings highlight the potential of language-based measures as non-invasive digital biomarkers for early AD risk stratification and for supporting clinical decision-making about biomarker testing for possible preclinical AD.

item.title: Multimodal MRI reveals brain structural and functional abnormalities associated with wearing-off phenomenon in Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
Neuroscience
OBJECTIVES: The pathogenesis of the wearing-off (WO) phenomenon in Parkinson's disease (PD) remains unclear. This study aims to explore the abnormalities in brain structure and function among PD patients with WO. METHODS: A total of 39 PD patients with wearing-off (PD-WO) and 43 PD patients without wearing-off (PD-nWO) were prospectively enrolled. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) was employed in this study to evaluate structural differences, and functional connectivity (FC) was used to assess functional differences between the two groups. RESULTS: Compared with PD-nWO patients, PD-WO patients showed significantly reduced gray matter volume (GMV) within the left middle occipital gyrus (MOG.L), bilateral middle temporal gyri (MTG.L/R), as well as the left triangular division of the inferior frontal gyrus (IFGtriang.L). Regarding functional connectivity, PD-WO patients exhibited widespread abnormalities, including weakened connectivity in the cerebellar-basal ganglia-sensorimotor cortex circuits, hippocampus-postcentral gyrus, and cerebellar-occipital (cuneal cortex) pathways, as well as enhanced connectivity between cerebellar subregions and between the cerebellum and occipital cortex (lingual gyrus) and parahippocampal gyrus. CONCLUSIONS: This preliminary single-center cross-sectional study revealed significant differences in brain structure and function between PD-WO and PD-nWO patients. These findings provide a better understanding of the neural mechanisms behind the WO phenomenon in PD and suggest potential therapeutic targets.

item.title: Quantitative anatomy of the human striatum suggests limited synaptic plasticity and higher structural stability in the intermediate putamen than in the nucleus accumbens.
item.description:
Neuroscience
The striatum is the input nucleus of the basal ganglia and receives convergent projections from the cerebral cortex, the thalamus, the amygdala, and the substantia nigra. The topographical organization of these synaptic projections provides the connective bases for the functional subdivision of the striatum into sensorimotor, associative, and limbic domains, that are largely homogeneous in cellular composition due to the predominance of medium spiny neurons. In spite of this homogeneity, there are several molecular, cellular, and biochemical differences that could contribute to the connection-based functional specialization and to differences in disease vulnerability between striatal sectors. In the present article we analyze postmortem striatal tissue from neurotypical human donors to identify cellular and molecular factors that could underlie functional specialization and selective vulnerability across the human striatum. We quantify neuronal morphological features related to genetic expression and protein synthesis, molecular markers that promote either synaptic plasticity or structural stability, and gene expression data in two striatal regions: the limbic nucleus accumbens and the sensorimotor intermediate putamen. Our analyses reveal larger neuron bodies, higher expression of markers that inhibit synaptic plasticity in the intermediate putamen and higher expression of markers thar promote synaptic plasticity in the nucleus accumbens. These findings support the notion that the intermediate putamen is characterized by enhanced structural stability and limited plastic potential, in contrast to the greater adaptability preserved in the nucleus accumbens.

item.title: Repetition Dissociates Pointer and Content-based Representations in Visual Working Memory: Contrasting the CDA with Multivariate Shape Decoding.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Memorizing a new phone number or address is hard at first, but becomes easier with repetition, as information shifts from working memory to long-term memory. Here we investigated how repetition affects the storage and transition of different aspects of mnemonic information by comparing univariate neural markers of active object storage with multivariate decoding of memory content. Thirty participants encoded lateralized stimuli from a continuous shape space into memory. Memory items were repeated six times in a row to induce learning. In line with earlier work, EEG recordings revealed that repetition led to a reduction in contralateral delay activity (CDA), a measure of active storage that has been taken to reflect a pointer-like representation of the individual object or its original source. In contrast, shape decoding during the retention and also after an impulse perturbation remained constant across repetitions. These results suggest that learning over repetitions reflects the abolishment of active and individuated object memory representations while passive, source-independent memory representations are retained.

item.title: Brain-heart decoupling in somatic depression: Desynchronization between salience network neuropsychological connectivity and heart rate variability.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Somatic depression is a distinct subtype of major depressive disorder, with a poorer response to treatment, an elevated risk of suicidal behaviour, and a worse prognosis. Interoception, the sense of internal bodily signals, is related to somatic symptoms. However, the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of body brain communication remain unclear. 293 depressed patients (145 with somatic symptoms and 148 without), and 160 healthy controls underwent magnetoencephalography during a resting state. Both the intra- and inter-network neural oscillation patterns of the salience network, were computed, alongside and heart rate variability (HRV) as a measure of autonomic function. Individuals with somatic depression exhibited lower HRV, accompanied by theta hyper-connectivity within the salience network. Although higher theta connectivity was linked to increased HRV in controls, this correlation was attenuated or even reversed in patients with somatic depression. Our findings identify a specific pattern of brain-heart decoupling in somatic depression, characterized by disrupted communication between salience network theta oscillations and autonomic cardiac regulation. This provides novel neuroimaging evidence for body-brain communication deficits in a clinically important depression subtype.

item.title: Temporal coupling shapes the effects of prolonged muscle-tendon vibration on sensorimotor EEG activity during motor imagery.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Motor imagery (MI) recruits sensorimotor networks overlapping those engaged during physical execution and represents a promising rehabilitation tool. While concurrent afferent stimulation enhances MI-related cortical engagement, the effects of prolonged proprioceptive conditioning prior to MI remain unexplored. This study investigated whether prolonged muscle-tendon vibration (MTV) could modulate cortical activity during subsequent MI, indexed by electroencephalographic alpha- and beta-band event-related desynchronization (ERD). Twenty healthy adults performed imagined maximal isometric knee extensions before and after 20-minute suprapatellar MTV (100 Hz) or SHAM vibration (30 Hz with foam interface) in counterbalanced sessions. Cortical engagement was assessed via EEG burst detection over central electrodes (C3, Cz, C4). Maximal force capacity, submaximal force estimation performance, and cortical responses during combined MI and MTV were also evaluated. MTV induced stronger vibratory responses than SHAM, consistent with enhanced proprioceptive afferent activation. Following MTV, voluntary force outcomes showed near-threshold changes consistent with the expected direction, namely reduced maximal force capacity and altered submaximal force calibration, suggesting modified proprioceptive feedback. MI performed after MTV conditioning exhibited reduced alpha- and beta-band ERD compared to SHAM, with greater vibratory-induced responses being associated with a less pronounced post-vibration beta ERD. Conversely, when MI was performed concurrently with MTV following conditioning, alpha-band ERD increased selectively in the MTV session, with no modulation in the beta band. These findings suggest that prolonged proprioceptive conditioning modulates MI-related cortical engagement differently depending on the sensorimotor context in which imagery is performed. Such state-dependent effects may support distinct intervention strategies aimed either at recalibrating maladaptive sensorimotor patterns or at enhancing cortical recruitment in rehabilitation contexts.

item.title: A transdiagnostic model of illness awareness and denial: Core components of the broader construct of insight into illness.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Insight into illness is a dynamic multidimensional construct that varies between individuals and medical and psychiatric disorders, and influences treatment engagement and clinical outcomes. Despite extensive study, accounts remain fragmented and disorder specific. This review focuses on subjective illness awareness and proposes a hypothesis-generating neurobiological framework in which fluctuations in awareness and denial emerge from interactions among self-representational networks, hierarchical predictive processing, and salience-threat systems that shape the balance between self-model stability and adaptation to illness-related information. Illness-related stimuli generate prediction errors (i.e., mismatches between sensory input and the self-model) that may update higher-order self-beliefs when assigned sufficient precision. Conversely, denial may occur when identity-relevant psychological threat biases precision toward self-related priors, potentially shifting network dynamics toward relatively left-lateralized self-representational states that attenuate discrepant information and preserve psychological homeostasis. This probabilistic model of illness awareness depends on the strength and credibility of illness-related evidence and flexibility of higher-order self-related beliefs. The review specifies falsifiable predictions for hemispheric engagement, threat-related precision weighting, and self-specific belief updating and identifies potential therapeutic targets.

item.title: Scanner acoustic noise in resting-state fMRI.
item.description:
Magnetic resonance imaging
Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) is usually acquired during rapid gradient switching that produces intense, spectrally structured sound. Scanner sound activates auditory pathways and can alter neural, vigilance, autonomic, respiratory, and movement-related states, but its sound-specific causal effect on intrinsic functional-connectivity estimates remains unresolved. Direct human comparisons are few and heterogeneous: some report stronger or more extensive network estimates under quieter acquisition, whereas others find broadly preserved topology and within-network connectivity. Near-silent Looping Star imaging can recover canonical resting-state networks with marked sound reduction, but reduced temporal signal-to-noise ratio and functional sensitivity expose a trade-off between acoustic burden and measurement performance.
