Most quiet-versus-standard contrasts simultaneously alter temporal sampling, gradient vibration, reconstruction, steady-state behavior, or image quality and therefore identify a total protocol effect rather than a sound-specific effect. A structured, original-scale comparison reports acoustic levels and metrics, measurement conditions, acquisition parameters, and resting-state outcomes without pooling unlike measures. Vigilance, autonomic activity, respiration, and movement are potential mediators; indiscriminate regression of these variables can remove part of the total acoustic effect. Current evidence establishes that acquisition protocols can alter rs-fMRI estimates and that scanner sound is biologically active, but it does not establish a universal, directionally uniform suppression of human resting-state connectivity by conventional echo-planar imaging. Future sound-specific attribution would require randomized within-subject manipulation, protected-ear frequency-resolved dosimetry, control of co-varying vibration and sequence properties, and synchronized state and physiological monitoring.

item.title: Degree-biased diffusion geometry of networks. Implications for network neurosciences.
item.description:
Mathematical biosciences
Degree-biased diffusion gives unequal directional influence to the two ends of an undirected edge. Its propagator is therefore nonsymmetric, and it generates two geometries. The column geometry compares the responses to perturbations at different sources, and the row geometry compares the observations across the same family of perturbations. We show that both geometries are Euclidean at finite times, but they can differ in their transient behavior and in their long-time limits. In contrast with standard diffusion, individual distances can expand temporarily even while the dynamics approach consensus. Degree-biased diffusion conserves a degree-weighted quantity instead of the ordinary network mass. An exact transport-and-reservoir decomposition identifies the local exchange responsible for this difference. Degree-biased Laplacians also arise exactly as the linearization of the dynamic mean-field model of large-scale brain activity when the long-range synaptic coupling is modulated by inverse receiver and sender gains. This gives them a neurobiological interpretation and a physical time scale. On a 76-region human structural connectome, degree bias changes the pairwise proximity, the geometrically optimal routes, and the regions visited by those routes. Hubs-attracting diffusion produces an earlier and higher maximum of column signature information than standard diffusion, while it reduces the row maximum. Hubs-repelling diffusion increases both maxima, but it reaches them later. The number of source responses needed to reconstruct the row kernel also depends strongly on the sampling order. In particular, high-degree sources are favored under attraction and low-degree sources under repulsion. These results characterize how a fixed network can generate distinct relational geometries under different propagation laws. Here, we treat geometric routes as distinct from literal signal trajectories, and mathematical reconstruction as distinct from evidence of conscious access.

item.title: A reproducible pipeline for simulating individual and inter-brain neural dynamics from structural connectivity.
item.description:
Journal of neuroscience methods
BACKGROUND: Computational models can link anatomical structure to neural dynamics. However, there is no validated, reproducible pipeline that simulates individual and inter-brain EEG-like dynamics from an individual's own structural connectome. NEW METHOD: To address this, we developed a comprehensive computational pipeline that combines probabilistic tractography from Diffusion Magnetic Resonance Imaging (dMRI) with dynamical systems modeling to simulate EEG-like neural dynamics from individual connectomes. It extracts anatomical connectivity, intra-individual functional connectivity, and inter-individual (two-brain) functional coupling features. It then evaluates their group-discriminative information with random-forest classification under repeated nested cross-validation. Simulated phase-locking values are calibrated against empirical resting-state EEG. RESULTS: In a test sample of individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and matched controls (16 each), simulated intra-individual synchrony added classification information beyond anatomy, raising accuracy from 71.2% (AUC 0.843) to 77.6% (AUC 0.871), in a sample where groups did not differ in mean structural connectivity. COMPARISON WITH EXISTING METHODS: Unlike current single-brain simulations, this pipeline generates and jointly simulates two individual brain models within a single system, and reports the contribution of each feature level explicitly. CONCLUSIONS: The pipeline provides a reproducible, extensible framework for deriving informative individual-level dynamic features from anatomy. The two-brain extension generates and ranks candidate inter-brain features, providing a principled way to identify between-brain measures for hypothesis-driven testing.

item.title: Exposure-Focused Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Increases Connectivity Between the Central Executive and Salience Networks in Pediatric Anxiety.
item.description:
Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
OBJECTIVE: Exposure is considered the most active element of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for pediatric anxiety. Yet many youth do not respond to CBT, and exposure is the component patients most often find difficult to tolerate. Cognitive control and its supporting neural substrates may enhance exposure efficacy by helping youth remain engaged with feared stimuli despite urges to avoid. However, little work has identified how exposure-based CBT modulates intrinsic connectivity of tripartite networks that support cognitive control (e.g., central executive [CEN], salience [SN], and default mode networks [DMN]), limiting efforts to develop strategies to improve and personalize treatment. Progress may be limited by individual variability in network connectivity in anxiety, which may obscure treatment-related effects in group-averaged analyses. This randomized clinical trial (RCT) leverages person-specific network modeling to test how exposure versus relaxation components of CBT influence resting-state connectivity of cognitive control networks in pediatric anxiety. METHOD: Youth aged 7-18 years with an anxiety disorder (N = 100) or low/no anxiety (L/NA; N = 35) completed resting-state fMRI scans at baseline. Patients were randomized to exposure-focused CBT (EF-CBT) or relaxation mentorship training (RMT). Resting-state connectivity was reassessed following treatment (or after a commensurate interval in L/NA youth) in 112 participants. Changes in within-CEN, CEN-SN, and CEN-DMN density were examined using Group Iterative Multiple Model Estimation, which yields sparse, person-specific networks capturing both shared and individual connectivity structure. RESULTS: At baseline, anxious youth exhibited lower density within-CEN and between CEN-DMN than L/NA youth. Treatment effects differed by intervention: EF-CBT selectively increased CEN-SN density, whereas RMT increased within-CEN density. CONCLUSION: These findings demonstrate dissociable effects of exposure and relaxation on cognitive control network organization in pediatric anxiety. These results indicate that exposure-focused CBT is uniquely associated with increased connectivity between control and salience systems, consistent with a mechanism supporting top-down control of threat-related signals during exposure. Person-specific measures of tripartite network connectivity may inform future efforts to identify candidate neural targets for optimizing and personalizing treatment.

item.title: Semantic Similarity-Related Neural Patterns and Their Associations with GABA-Glutamate Levels in the Left Inferior Frontal Gyrus, Anterior Temporal Lobe, and Inferior Parietal Lobule.
item.description:
Biological psychology
It remains unclear how graded lexical-semantic similarity between prime-target pairs is reflected in mean BOLD responses and multivariate neural activity patterns, and how these neural indices relate to regional GABA, Glx (glutamate + glutamine), and GABA/Glx levels. We examined the neural correlates of lexical-semantic similarity and their associations with regional neurochemical measures in 46 healthy adults using fMRI during a semantic priming task and magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) acquired on a separate day. Trial-wise prime-target semantic similarity was quantified using word-vector cosine similarity. Similarity-related BOLD responses were assessed using parametric modulation, whereas neural-semantic correspondence was examined using representational similarity analysis (RSA). Semantic similarity modulated BOLD activity primarily under incongruency, involving premotor, dorsolateral prefrontal, frontal eye field, angular gyrus, and anterior prefrontal regions. ROI-based RSA revealed FWE-corrected neural-semantic correspondence in the left inferior frontal gyrus pars opercularis (IFG-Op) and medial superior frontal gyrus. Within-condition analyses further showed distributed neural-semantic correspondence under incongruency across frontal, temporal, and parietal regions implicated in semantic control and integration processes, including bilateral IFG and the left inferior parietal lobule (IPL). Additionally, a positive association was observed between RSA model fit and left IPL Glx levels in the incongruent condition, although this association did not survive FDR correction. Together, these findings suggest that lexical-semantic similarity is reflected in condition-dependent neural responses and representational geometry and may represent an additional dimension modulating semantic control demands, while evidence for associations with regional neurochemical measures remains preliminary.

item.title: Posterior fossa syndrome.
item.description:
Child's nervous system : ChNS : official journal of the International Society for Pediatric Neurosurgery
Posterior fossa syndrome (PFS), also known as cerebellar mutism syndrome (CMS), is a distressing postoperative complication affecting children undergoing craniotomy for infratentorial tumors, most frequently medulloblastoma. It is characterized by a distinct latency period followed by mutism, profound emotional dysregulation, and a broad spectrum of cerebellar motor and cognitive deficits. Diffusion MRI and tractography have consistently shown that structural damage to the proximal efferent cerebellar pathway-specifically the dentato-rubro-thalamo-cortical tract within the superior cerebellar peduncle-is strongly implicated as the anatomical driver of PFS. Historical series favored the telovelar over the transvermian surgical approach, although recent prospective multicenter data demonstrate equivalent risks between the two techniques, shifting the neurosurgical focus toward meticulous surgical technique and minimizing damage to eloquent tissue around the fourth ventricle. Validated clinical scoring tools, such as the Posterior Fossa Syndrome Questionnaire, standardize clinical phenotyping and are making their way into clinical practice. Increasingly advanced risk prediction models allow for precise preoperative risk stratification based on objective imaging markers. Pharmacological interventions, including zolpidem and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, have shown limited efficacy in mitigating acute symptoms. Although near-universal clinical improvement occurs over time, long-term neurocognitive and motor sequelae remain highly disabling. Combining advanced neuroimaging, sophisticated risk modeling and meticulous microsurgical technique offers the best paradigm to shift the narrative of PFS from an expected complication to a preventable one.
